content.problem: A matrix multiplication appears in your Python code, but what reaches the compiler and what might limit its speed? We will inspect a lowered program, calculate an explicit work/traffic model, and compare that model with synchronized CPU measurements without confusing a ceiling with a prediction.
content.idea: A roofline compares arithmetic work with data movement under stated compute and bandwidth assumptions. It helps us predict which resource may constrain a workload. It is a model to test against measurements, not a hardware benchmark by itself.
objectives: Locate matrix multiplication and activation in StableHLO.
Derive the operation and minimum byte counts for a declared matrix contract.
Identify the compute-versus-bandwidth transition in a hypothetical roofline.
Explain why measured throughput can fall below either ceiling.

sections.title: Read a roofline as a conditional bound
sections.body:
A roofline turns two assumed budgets into a conditional ceiling. With 100 GB/s bandwidth and 1000 GFLOP/s compute, the curves meet at 10 FLOP/byte. At intensity 2 FLOP/byte, the bandwidth line gives 200 GFLOP/s, so the lower of the two budgets is the bound for this model.

This is a hypothetical calculation, not a performance result. Use it to predict whether more reuse could raise the modeled bound; verify any implementation change with compiler output and a synchronized measurement of the same workload.

check.prompt: Does reaching the compute-limited side guarantee peak throughput?
check.answer: No. It identifies the tighter bound in this model. Other bottlenecks and inefficient execution can keep observed performance far below it.

sections.title: Read the contract before the compiler text
sections.body: The measured example multiplies \((32,16)\) by \((16,8)\), yielding \((32,8)\), then applies tanh. Lowering this specific input contract produces StableHLO containing `dot_general` and `tanh` in the recorded run. Read these operation meanings and tensor types before interpreting compiler cost fields; names and lowering details can vary by version and backend.

sections.title: Count work with a stated convention
sections.body:
For dimensions \(m,k,n\), count one multiply and one addition per inner-product term: \(2mkn\) floating-point operations. For the declared matrix shapes, that gives 8192 matmul operations. The count omits tanh and uses a conventional two-operations-per-term accounting, so label its scope if you turn it into a throughput estimate.

Compiler estimates report a separate backend-specific view of work. Neither one is a measured device trace.

sections.title: Minimum traffic is an assumption you can challenge
sections.body:
Assume each float32 input is read once and the output is written once. The matrix shapes then imply \(4(32\cdot16+16\cdot8+32\cdot8)=3584\) bytes and intensity \(8192/3584=16/7\approx2.29\) operations per byte for matmul-only work.

This minimum omits tanh, intermediates, repeated reads, cache effects and layout changes. It is an accounting assumption that you can challenge with compiler estimates or traffic evidence, not a claim that exactly 3584 bytes moved.

sections.title: Find the corner in a hypothetical roofline
sections.body:
The plotted roofline assumes 100 billion operations/s and 20 billion bytes/s, so the transition is at 5 operations/byte. Below that ridge, the bandwidth ceiling rises with intensity; above it, the combined ceiling stays at the compute cap. For the square-size cases, the first two plotted bounds are about 26.67 and 53.33 GFLOP/s; at intensity 5 the model reaches 100 GFLOP/s.

Use that slope change to predict the effect of doubling reuse in a bandwidth-limited case. It raises the modeled bound only until the compute ceiling; it does not guarantee a faster measured program.

sections.title: Compare measurements only after checking equivalence
sections.body:
The executable is compared with an independent NumPy product and tanh, then warmed and timed with output synchronization. The recorded CPU samples vary substantially, which is expected to matter for this tiny workload; the calculation's hypothetical GFLOP/s ceilings are not measured CPU throughput.

For a real roofline, select budgets for the actual device and precision, name the memory level, and gather traffic evidence. Keep dtype, shape and operation equivalent when comparing measured results.

content.output: StableHLO contains the declared dot and activation. The matmul accounting is \(8192\) operations and \(3584\) minimum bytes; the hypothetical ceilings begin near \(26.67\), \(53.33\), then \(100\) GFLOP/s. CPU times vary.

experiments.title: Double the assumed data movement
experiments.prediction: If effective traffic doubles without changing arithmetic work, how does the intensity and modeled ceiling change?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Double the assumed data movement: The work is unchanged; doubling transferred bytes halves intensity.
reduced=intensity/2
revised=np.minimum(peak,bandwidth*reduced)
np.testing.assert_allclose(revised[:2],roofline[:2]/2)
assert revised[-1]==peak
print('Ceilings with twice minimum traffic GFLOP/s:',(revised/1e9).tolist())
experiments.output: The first bandwidth-limited ceilings halve; a sufficiently intense case stays compute-limited.
experiments.explanation: The work is unchanged; doubling transferred bytes halves intensity. This is a sensitivity calculation, not a measured cache miss rate.

content.exercise: Derive the work and minimum traffic for shapes \((48,24)\) and \((24,12)\). Compare your hand calculation with the contract function and report the hypothetical limiting budget.
content.solution:
# Exercise solution: Derive the work and minimum traffic for shapes (48,24) and (24,12).
work,traffic,ratio=contract(48,24,12)
assert work==27648 and traffic==8064
np.testing.assert_allclose(ratio,24/7)
assert bandwidth*ratio<peak
print('Changed contract:',work,traffic,ratio,'bandwidth-limited in the hypothetical model')

practice.title: Keep the same shapes but change storage precision
practice.prompt: Change only the assumed element size from four bytes to two bytes. Calculate the resulting traffic and intensity, and explain why this is insufficient to predict an actual speedup.
practice.hint: The model assumes both inputs and output use that element size; real accumulation and conversion may differ.
practice.solution:
# Keep the same shapes but change storage precision (Transfer)
f32,b32,i32=contract(32,16,8,4)
f16,b16,i16=contract(32,16,8,2)
assert f32==f16 and b32==2*b16
np.testing.assert_allclose(i16,2*i32)
print('Arithmetic unchanged; modeled traffic halved and intensity doubled.')
practice.explanation: Changing storage bytes in an accounting model is separate from native arithmetic support, accumulation policy, quality preservation or measured runtime improvement.

content.question: The lowered program contains a dot operation and a roofline model predicts a high ceiling. What is still needed before claiming high accelerator throughput?
options: A matching measured workload on the actual device, with justified traffic and precision assumptions.
Only the number of Python source lines.
content.explanation: A typed intermediate representation and an optimistic ceiling do not measure execution. Workload equivalence, synchronization, device evidence and appropriate model assumptions are still required.
content.diagnosis: If a roofline claim looks implausible, check operation-count convention, byte units, element size, memory level and timing boundary. Inspect compiler estimates separately from measured traffic; neither should be silently relabeled as the other.
takeaways: Lowered text describes a specialized program, not a timeline.
Arithmetic intensity depends on an explicit traffic model.
A roofline is a ceiling under assumptions, not a promised runtime.

visual.title: A hypothetical roofline bends at the compute budget
visual.prediction: Which square-matrix cases lie below the transition intensity?
visual.reading: The x-axis is minimum-traffic arithmetic intensity in operations per byte; the y-axis is a hypothetical ceiling in GFLOP/s. The bandwidth series rises as intensity times the assumed 20 GB/s, the compute series stays at 100 GFLOP/s, and the combined curve follows the lower series. These lines are model budgets, not device measurements. The first two cases give about 26.67 and 53.33 GFLOP/s; at the ridge of 5 operations/byte, the ceiling reaches 100.
visual.connection: The plotted square cases use a simple one-read/one-write traffic estimate: larger matrices have higher modeled reuse, so their bandwidth ceiling rises until it meets the compute cap. The lesson's rectangular matmul separately has modeled intensity \(16/7\approx2.29\) operations/byte under the same minimum-traffic convention; compare that location with the curve only as an estimate. Next predict whether doubling the modeled intensity would remain below the ridge, then measure an equivalent implementation before claiming improvement.
visual.alt: Hypothetical bandwidth and compute ceilings with their minimum; the first two cases are bandwidth-limited.

content.code:
# Step 1 — Inspect a specialized lowered computation: StableHLO establishes the operation and shape contract.
import time
import numpy as np
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

# Step 2 — Calculate an explicitly hypothetical model
def workload(a,b):return jnp.tanh(a@b)
a=jnp.arange(32*16,dtype=jnp.float32).reshape(32,16)/512
b=jnp.arange(16*8,dtype=jnp.float32).reshape(16,8)/128
# Wrap with `jax.jit` (`lowered`) so XLA traces and compiles the function.
lowered=jax.jit(workload).lower(a,b)
# Trace or lower the function to inspect its compiler representation (`stablehlo`).
stablehlo=str(lowered.compiler_ir(dialect='stablehlo'))
assert 'dot_general' in stablehlo and 'tanh' in stablehlo
# Trace or lower the function to inspect its compiler representation (`executable`).
executable=lowered.compile()
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
np.testing.assert_allclose(executable(a,b),np.tanh(np.asarray(a)@np.asarray(b)),rtol=2e-5,atol=2e-5)
print('StableHLO operations present: dot_general and tanh')
print('Compiler estimates (backend-specific):',executable.cost_analysis())

# An analytic traffic model, not a measurement of this CPU.
def contract(m,k,n,itemsize=4):
    if min(m,k,n,itemsize)<=0:raise ValueError('positive dimensions and itemsize required')
    flops=2*m*k*n  # conventional multiply-add count; excludes tanh
    minimum_bytes=itemsize*(m*k+k*n+m*n)
    return flops,minimum_bytes,flops/minimum_bytes
sizes=np.array([8,16,32,64,128])
intensity=np.array([contract(int(n),int(n),int(n))[2] for n in sizes])
np.testing.assert_allclose(intensity,sizes/6)
peak=100e9
bandwidth=20e9  # hypothetical budgets, not device specifications
memory_ceiling=bandwidth*intensity
roofline=np.minimum(peak,memory_ceiling)
np.testing.assert_allclose(roofline[:2]/1e9,[80/3,160/3])
assert np.all(roofline[2:]==peak)

# Step 4 — Keep runtime observations separate
executable(a,b).block_until_ready()
times=[]
for _ in range(5):
    # Wait for device work to finish before timing it or comparing its result on the host.
    # Wait for device work to finish before timing it or comparing its result on the host.
    # Wait for device work to finish before timing it or comparing its result on the host.
    start=time.perf_counter()
    executable(a,b).block_until_ready()
    times.append(time.perf_counter()-start)
flops,minimum_bytes,ai=contract(32,16,8)
print('Local CPU samples seconds:',times)
print('Matmul-only accounting:',{'flops':flops,'minimum_bytes':minimum_bytes,'flops_per_byte':ai})
print('Hypothetical ceilings GFLOP/s:',(roofline/1e9).tolist())
